chunks.title: Why graft? Donors & prognosis
chunks.tldr: Graft reasons: optical, tectonic, therapeutic, cosmetic. Best prognosis: keratoconus, small scars, dystrophies. Worst: vascularised, numb, inflamed corneas.
points: Optical: keratoconus, scars, dystrophies, pseudophakic bullous keratopathy.
Tectonic: keep the eye intact (descemetocoele, thinning).
Therapeutic: remove infected tissue that won't respond.
Donor: retrieve within 12–24 h of death. Infant corneas (≤3 years) rarely used. Stored cold (7–10 days) or in organ culture (4 weeks).

No donation if: unknown cause of death, HIV/hepatitis/syphilis/TB/sepsis, high-risk behaviour, CJD and other CNS diseases (dementia, MS, Parkinson, MND), pituitary growth hormone, most blood cancers, retinoblastoma, prior refractive surgery.
Poor-prognosis host: deep vessels, no sensation, very thin edge, active inflammation, lid disease, atopy/OCP, dry eye, PAS, uncontrolled glaucoma, uveitis. Fix what you can first.

cards.q: Name a CNS condition that excludes corneal donation.
cards.a: Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (also dementia, MS, Parkinson, MND).

chunks.title: Penetrating keratoplasty (PK)
chunks.tldr: Full-thickness graft, usually 7.5 mm, donor 0.25 mm bigger. Long-term topical steroid. Remove loose sutures immediately (rejection risk).
points: Smaller grafts → astigmatism. Bigger → PAS, high IOP, rejection.
Cut the donor first, then the host (in case the donor is unusable).
Continuous or interrupted sutures (or both).
After: pred 1% / dex 2-hourly → taper → once daily for a year or more. Cycloplegic 1–2 weeks. Oral aciclovir if HSV history. Check IOP (non-applanation early).
Sutures out at 12–18 months (longer in elderly). Loose/broken sutures out now.
Early complications: epithelial defect, loose sutures, wound leak, uveitis, high IOP, rupture, CMO, infection, endophthalmitis, Urrets-Zavalia (fixed dilated pupil).
Late: astigmatism, disease recurs, wound dehiscence, retrocorneal membrane, glaucoma, rejection, failure.
chunks.hook: Loose suture = welcome mat for vessels and rejection.

cards.q: Why prepare the donor button before excising host tissue?
cards.a: So surgery isn't left incomplete if the donor proves unusable.

chunks.title: Graft rejection
chunks.tldr: Red, blurry, sore graft = rejection until proven otherwise. Khodadoust line (endothelial, worst), Krachmer spots (subepithelial). Treat with hourly topical steroid ± IV methylprednisolone.
points: Cornea is immune-privileged (no vessels/lymphatics). Lost with vessels, inflammation.
Risks: big (>8 mm) or eccentric grafts, host vessels, infection (HSV), glaucoma, previous grafts. Male donor → female recipient is worse. HLA matching helps a little.
Symptoms: blur, redness, photophobia, pain (may be silent). Days to years later.
Epithelial: raised epithelial line (~3 months).
Subepithelial: Krachmer spots (like adenovirus infiltrates) on the donor.
Stromal: deeper haze.
Endothelial: Khodadoust line (line of KPs) moving across from the vascularised edge + oedema.
Treat: preservative-free steroid hourly for 24 h → taper. Cycloplegic. Oral pred 1 mg/kg, or IV methylpred 500 mg (within 8 days). Subconj steroid, ciclosporin, tacrolimus.
Differentials: failure without inflammation, infection (HSV, fungus), uveitis, suture reaction, epithelial ingrowth.
chunks.hook: Khodadoust = Kills the endothelium (line of KPs). Krachmer = subepithelial spots.

chunks.title: Lamellar grafts: DALK, DSAEK, DMEK
chunks.tldr: Replace only the sick layer. Front sick → DALK (keep own endothelium = no endothelial rejection). Back sick (Fuchs) → DSAEK / DMEK (fast recovery, few sutures).
points: Superficial lamellar: front ⅓ scars, peripheral thinning (Terrien, recurrent pterygium, dermoid), descemetocoele patch.
DALK: remove almost down to Descemet. For keratoconus (no past hydrops), anterior scars, atopic patients (high rejection risk).
DALK pros: no endothelial rejection, stronger eye, less astigmatism, any donor endothelium OK, sutures out ~6 months.
DALK cons: hard, risk of perforating Descemet, interface haze.
DSAEK: strip host Descemet/endothelium, insert donor endothelium + a thin stromal layer through a small incision. Most common.
DMEK: Descemet + endothelium only (5–10 µm). Best vision, lowest rejection, harder surgery.
EK pros: small refractive change, strong eye, fast recovery. Cons: learning curve, equipment, endothelial rejection still possible.

cards.a: No risk of endothelial rejection (host endothelium retained).

cards.q: Which EK technique transplants only Descemet + endothelium?

chunks.title: Limbal stem cell grafts & keratoprosthesis
chunks.tldr: Stem cell deficiency = goblet cells on the cornea (conjunctivalisation), vessels, persistent defects. One eye → autograft from the good eye. Both → allograft. End-stage → keratoprosthesis (OOKP).
points: LSCD signs: conjunctivalisation with goblet cells (impression cytology, CK19), vessels, pannus, persistent defects, scarring.
Causes: aniridia, chemical/thermal burns, SJS, OCP, surface tumours, contact lenses.
Fix lids, conjunctiva, IOP first. Partial → sector epitheliectomy + sector graft.
Total one-sided → autologous limbal graft from the other eye. Total both sides → living related or cadaver allograft. Also cultured (ex vivo) stem cells.
In one-sided SJS/OCP, don't take tissue from the 'good' eye.
Keratoprosthesis (osteo-odonto-keratoprosthesis = tooth + bone + optic cylinder): both eyes blind from end-stage surface disease (SJS, OCP, burns, trachoma), VA ≤CF, retina/nerve OK, motivated.
KPro complications: glaucoma (up to 75%), membranes, extrusion, RD, endophthalmitis. ~80% get CF to 6/12.
chunks.hook: Goblet cells on the cornea = the stem-cell fence is broken.

cards.q: Key sign of limbal stem cell deficiency on impression cytology?
cards.a: Goblet cells on the corneal surface (conjunctivalisation).

chunks.title: Refractive options by error
chunks.tldr: Rough limits: PRK myopia ~6 D, astig ~3 D. LASIK myopia ~12 D, hyperopia ~4 D, astig ~5 D. Beyond that → phakic IOL or lens exchange.
points: Myopia: surface ablation (low–moderate), LASIK (moderate–high), SMILE, clear lens exchange (RD risk in high myopes), iris-claw phakic IOL, ICL (posterior chamber phakic, −3 to −20.5 D). Radial keratotomy = historical.
Phakic IOL risks: endothelial loss, cataract, pupil block, uveitis, RD, oval pupil (iris claw).
Hyperopia: PRK (low), LASIK (≤4 D), conductive keratoplasty (radiofrequency), holmium laser thermal keratoplasty, lens surgery.
Astigmatism: limbal relaxing / arcuate incisions on the steep axis, PRK (~3 D), LASIK (~5 D), toric IOL (can rotate).
Presbyopia: multifocal/accommodating IOLs (glare, ~10% exchanged; may bar pilots), monovision, CK, corneal inlays, corneal multifocality.
Stop soft CLs 2 weeks, rigid lenses ≥3 weeks before measurements.
chunks.hook: Small error → laser the surface. Medium → flap (LASIK). Big → put a lens in.

chunks.title: LASIK
chunks.tldr: Flap → excimer reshapes the bed → flap back. Leave a residual bed ≥250 µm (ectasia risk). Watch for DLK ('sands of the Sahara'), epithelial ingrowth, flap problems.
points: Myopia: flatten the centre. Hyperopia: ablate the periphery (steepen the centre).
Suction ring (IOP shoots up) → microkeratome or femtosecond laser flap.
Pros vs PRK: more comfortable, faster recovery, less haze, larger corrections.
Cons: flap complications.
During: buttonhole, free cap, incomplete flap, AC entry.
After: dry eye (almost everyone), flap wrinkles/striae/dislocation, haze/glare, epithelial ingrowth, infection.
Diffuse lamellar keratitis: day 1–7, granular 'sand' at the interface → intensive topical steroid + antibiotic.
Ectasia: risk from forme fruste keratoconus and thin residual bed → screen topography first.
chunks.hook: DLK = Desert in the flap (Sahara sand) → steroids.

cards.q: Minimum residual stromal bed after LASIK ablation?
Granular interface deposits 1–7 days after LASIK?
cards.a: Diffuse lamellar keratitis ('sands of the Sahara').

chunks.title: PRK/LASEK & SMILE
chunks.tldr: PRK = remove epithelium, laser the surface. No flap → safer for thin corneas, contact sports, EBMD, but sore and slower. SMILE = femtosecond lenticule out through a 4 mm cut.
points: Corrects myopia ~6 D, astigmatism ~3 D, low hyperopia.
Epithelium off (sponge, brush, alcohol) → excimer to Bowman/stroma (30–60 s, eye tracking) → bandage CL → heals in 48–72 h.
Haze within 2 weeks (lasts weeks–months). Mitomycin C reduces it.
Choose PRK over LASIK: thin cornea, high injury risk (sports, military), EBMD, previous graft or RK, large pupils.
Complications: slow healing, haze, glare/haloes, regression, decentration, infection.
Variants: LASEK (alcohol, epithelium flap replaced), Epi-LASIK (epikeratome), Trans-PRK (laser removes the epithelium).
SMILE / ReLEx: femtosecond cuts a lenticule inside the cornea, removed via a small incision. Less nerve and biomechanical disruption, fewer flap issues.
chunks.hook: PRK = Pain Recovers Kinda slowly, but no flap to lose.

cards.q: Name 2 reasons to choose PRK over LASIK.
cards.a: Thin cornea; high risk of eye trauma (also EBMD, previous graft/RK, large pupil).
